title: Loosen a nylon nut with an adjustable wrench, rolling the jaw snug on the flats first
instruction: Loosen the nut on the base plate with the adjustable wrench, then take the wrench off it and set it down.
context: General maintenance and repair workers (about 1.6 million US jobs, O*NET 49-9071: "Dismantle machines, equipment, or devices to access and remove defective parts, using ... hand tools") and electricians (821,000) take apart equipment held by nylon nuts, used where a fastener must insulate or not corrode. A nylon nut's service torque is close to its failure torque: an M5 nylon 6/6 nut is tightened to 0.73-0.79 N*m and fails at 0.93 N*m, so a wrench whose jaw is left loose bears on the soft corners and can shave or mark them near service load. Before pulling, the worker rolls the knurled worm until the movable jaw is snug on the flats, and pulls so the nut presses into the fixed jaw, solid with the handle; pulled the other way the load lands on the movable jaw's tip. Safety agencies' hand-tool guidance gives both rules. Here the jaw is 1 mm too wide.
setup: Coordinates in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Angles are counterclockwise from +x, seen from above. Steel equipment mounting plate (fixed): 26 x 30 x 0.8 cm, painted blue-gray, centered at (27, 4), with a bolt head at each corner. Stud: M5 stainless, its axis at (30, 0), standing 0.4 cm above the nut. On it, a zinc M5 flat washer (DIN 125, 1.0 cm across, 0.1 cm thick) and an M5 hex nut of natural (off-white) nylon 6/6 (DIN 934, 0.8 cm across flats, 0.92 cm across corners, 0.4 cm thick; a fresh one each trial, so its corners are checked from new), tightened to 0.76 N*m, its maker's recommended torque (0.73-0.79 N*m; it fails at 0.93 N*m), with a torque screwdriver set to 0.76 N*m, never by hand, then left 5 minutes because nylon relaxes; every tenth nut is instead broken loose with a peak-hold torque screwdriver and the readings are reported. In the sim it turns on the stud once 0.76 N*m is reached and can be forced at most 10 degrees tighter. Adjustable wrench: 8-inch (20.5 cm), chrome steel, 0.25 kg, red dipped grip on the last 9 cm of the handle. It lies flat on the washer with the nut in the lower 4 mm of its 10 mm jaws, flats square to the jaws, its handle pointing from the nut toward 60 degrees (forward-left) and its jaw opening facing 330 degrees (forward-right). Its fixed jaw is on the far side of the nut from the handle; the movable jaw sits between the nut and the handle. The jaw is open 0.9 cm, 1 mm wider than the nut. The knurled worm (thumbwheel, 1.6 cm across, 1.1 cm long, its axis along the jaw's travel) sits in a window in the head 3.8 cm from the nut's axis toward the handle and stands 3 mm proud of the head's faces; one turn moves the jaw 2 mm, and rolling the worm's top toward the head's back (the throat side, away from the jaw opening) closes the jaw. Seen from above, a counterclockwise pull (handle end moving back and to the left) loosens the nut and presses it into the fixed jaw; clockwise tightens it and loads the movable jaw. The wrench comes off by lifting it straight up along the stud, with no need to open the jaw; its jaws clear the stud's end once it is 1.6 cm up. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: Loosened: how far the nut turned counterclockwise on its stud from its start. Play: the jaw opening minus the nut's 0.8 cm across flats. Let go (a release check): no gripper has its tool point within 5 cm of the wrench's handle or head with its fingers under 60 % open. Set down: the wrench lifted off the nut and lying on the plate with its jaws 3 cm or more from the nut's axis. The trial scores 1.0 when the nut is loosened 60 degrees or more (one flat of the hex, a full swing) and the wrench is set down and let go. It scores 0.5 when the nut is loosened 60 degrees or more but the wrench is not set down: it is still on the nut, in the way of spinning it off by hand. It scores 0.25 when the nut is loosened 5 to 60 degrees: a snug jaw and the right pull broke it loose, but less than one swing. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing, a nut loosened under 5 degrees (within the jaws' play and the thread's flex), a wrench not let go at the end (the job is not finished while the hand is on it), or either fault below. Faults (0 for the whole trial) are operational proxies, not a validated measurement of rounding. Loose-jaw pull, the proxy for jaw slip and corner damage: the nut turned 2 degrees or more in total over every pull, while the play was over 0.4 mm, or the wrench turned 30 degrees round a nut its jaws cannot grip (play over 1.24 mm). With 0.4 mm of play the 8 mm nut turns 5.4 degrees in the jaws before they bear, on its corners, which a steel jaw can shave or mark on a nylon nut near service torque; a new wrench's jaw clearance is at most 0.25 mm (ISO 6787). Movable jaw loaded: the nut forced 2 degrees or more clockwise while the wrench is on it, a tightening pull loading the movable jaw's tip. The nut moves only after 3.4 degrees of wrench flex, so 2 degrees is a real tightening pull. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Real trial: a camera fixed 25 cm above the nut films the whole run. In every frame a video angle tool reads the nut's turn from a paint line across its top against a line on the plate, and the play from a fine line on the movable jaw against a 0.5 mm scale on the head, zeroed on the flats and checked with 0.4 mm and 1 mm feeler gauges, through every pull and worm adjustment. Secondary check: square-on photos of the nut before and after at the same magnification and light; a new flattening or burr on a corner also counts as a loose-jaw pull. The wrench's final position is taken with a tape measure.
reset_notes: Thread a fresh nylon M5 nut on the stud and tighten it with the torque screwdriver set to 0.76 N*m; wait 5 minutes (nylon relaxes) and start the trial. Every tenth nut, instead of a trial, measure its breakaway with a peak-hold torque screwdriver and log it (README). Photograph its flats from above. Set the wrench on it with its flats square in the jaws and the handle toward 60 degrees, and open the jaw to 9.0 mm with a caliper (1 mm of play).
fidelity: The wrench rides hidden joints (lift, turn about the nut, two slides): it can be lifted off and laid flat but not tipped. The nut turns on its stud through a modeled thread that breaks loose at 0.76 N*m, an M5 nylon nut's service torque (5.8 N at 13 cm). It cannot deform: turning it with over 0.4 mm of play is an operational proxy for jaw slip and corner damage, not validated rounding; a real trial reads play and turn from video, with corner photos as a second check.
